items.prompt:
(1) Why must pressure be considered when comparing a water sample’s boiling point with 100 °C?
A. Pure water boils independently of pressure
B. Impurities alone change the boiling temperature
C. Pressure can change the boiling temperature
D. Reduced pressure demonstrates increased dissolved impurity [1]

(2) What is soap scum?
A. Insoluble calcium or magnesium soap
B. A soluble sodium or potassium soap
C. An emulsion of pure soap and air
D. A deposit of calcium carbonate only [1]

(3) Why can washing soda soften calcium sulfate water?
A. Sulfate precipitates while calcium remains dissolved
B. Carbonate ions precipitate dissolved calcium ions
C. Calcium sulfate changes into calcium metal
D. Dissolved calcium ions are trapped directly by filter paper [1]

(4) Why may fertiliser improve growth in nutrient-deficient soil?
A. It supplies energy to replace photosynthesis
B. It increases growth irrespective of soil composition
C. It supplies deficient mineral nutrients
D. It removes the need for water uptake [1]

(5) Why does shortage of irrigation water threaten crop production?
A. Irrigation water is the main source of plant carbon
B. Less irrigation removes the need for mineral nutrients
C. Dry conditions increase photosynthesis regardless of species
D. Water is needed for plant processes and growth [1]

(6) Which pairing correctly explains carbon dioxide formation?
A. Metal + dilute acid → salt + CO2
B. Acid + carbonate → salt + CO2 + water
C. Metal hydroxide + acid → salt + CO2
D. Hydrocarbon + excess oxygen → carbon + hydrogen [1]

(7) Why is oxygen used in steelmaking?
A. It reduces iron oxide directly to pure iron
B. It prevents oxidation of carbon impurities
C. It oxidises impurities in molten material
D. It supplies the carbon needed for steel [1]

(8) Why is carbon monoxide especially dangerous in a confined space?
A. It is detected reliably by smell
B. It supplies extra oxygen to blood
C. It is a harmless visible dust
D. It accumulates and impairs oxygen transport [1]

(9) Which process can produce methane?
A. Oxygen-poor decomposition of vegetation
B. Aerobic respiration of glucose
C. Complete combustion of methane
D. Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate [1]

(10) Which conversion is promoted by a suitable vehicle catalytic converter?
A. CO2 to CO
B. N2 to NO2
C. CO to solid carbon
D. CO to CO2 [1]

(11) What happens when limestone is strongly heated to form lime?
A. CaCO3 absorbs CO2 while producing CaO
B. CaCO3 decomposes to CaO and CO2
C. CaCO3 loses oxygen but retains all its carbon
D. CaCO3 reacts with water to form CaO [1]

(12) Why is an iron catalyst used in the Haber process?
A. It speeds the approach to equilibrium
B. It increases equilibrium yield at fixed temperature
C. It is consumed to supply nitrogen to ammonia
D. It makes pressure unnecessary for the equilibrium choice [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) C. Pressure can change the boiling temperature. Boiling occurs when vapour pressure matches the external pressure.
Distractor explanations: A: Even pure water has a pressure-dependent boiling point. B: Pressure as well as impurities can change boiling temperature. D: A pressure change is not evidence of dissolved impurity.

(2) A. Insoluble calcium or magnesium soap Hardness ions form insoluble soap compounds.
Distractor explanations: B: Soluble sodium/potassium soaps are not the insoluble scum. C: Scum is an insoluble compound, not simply trapped air. D: Calcium carbonate is not the calcium/magnesium soap precipitate.

(3) B. Carbonate ions precipitate dissolved calcium ions. Precipitation removes calcium from solution even though boiling is ineffective.
Distractor explanations: A: The calcium is precipitated as carbonate; sulfate remains in solution. C: Washing soda does not reduce calcium ions to calcium metal. D: Dissolved calcium ions pass through ordinary filter paper; precipitation must occur first.

(4) C. It supplies deficient mineral nutrients Fertiliser can correct a limiting mineral-nutrient supply.
Distractor explanations: A: Mineral nutrients do not replace light energy for photosynthesis. B: Benefit depends on which nutrient is limiting and how much is supplied. D: Plants still require water after fertiliser is added.

(5) D. Water is needed for plant processes and growth Water availability can limit growth and crop yield.
Distractor explanations: A: Most plant carbon comes from atmospheric CO2 rather than irrigation water. B: Water shortage does not remove mineral requirements. C: Dryness can limit growth; it does not universally increase photosynthesis.

(6) B. Acid + carbonate → salt + CO2 + water Acid–carbonate reaction releases CO2 from carbonate.
Distractor explanations: A: Suitable metals with dilute non-oxidising acid produce hydrogen, not CO2. C: Hydroxide neutralisation produces salt and water, not CO2. D: Complete combustion gives CO2 and water, not carbon and hydrogen.

(7) C. It oxidises impurities in molten material Controlled oxidation helps remove impurities.
Distractor explanations: A: Oxygen oxidises; it is not a reducing agent for iron oxide. B: Oxidation of excess carbon is one purpose of the oxygen. D: Oxygen does not supply carbon.

(8) D. It accumulates and impairs oxygen transport CO can accumulate without obvious sensory warning and bind haemoglobin.
Distractor explanations: A: Carbon monoxide is odourless, so smell is unreliable. B: It impairs oxygen transport rather than supplying oxygen. C: It is a toxic gas, not harmless visible dust.

(9) A. Oxygen-poor decomposition of vegetation Anaerobic decomposition can generate methane.
Distractor explanations: B: Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water. C: Complete combustion consumes methane rather than produces it. D: Heating calcium carbonate produces calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.

(10) D. CO to CO2 Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide.
Distractor explanations: A: This reverses the desired oxidation and produces toxic CO. B: This forms a pollutant rather than reducing nitrogen oxides. C: The specified conversion oxidises CO to CO2, not solid carbon.

(11) B. CaCO3 decomposes to CaO and CO2 Thermal decomposition releases CO2 and leaves CaO.
Distractor explanations: A: Heating releases carbon dioxide rather than absorbing it. C: Carbon leaves as CO2 rather than all remaining in the solid. D: Limestone decomposes on heating; adding water is not this reaction.

(12) A. It speeds the approach to equilibrium A catalyst increases reaction rates without changing equilibrium position. This concerns the gaseous Haber equilibrium.
Distractor explanations: B: A catalyst does not alter equilibrium yield at fixed conditions. C: Iron is not consumed as a nitrogen source. D: Pressure still affects the gaseous equilibrium yield.

items.prompt:
(a) Describe how adding washing soda can soften calcium sulfate water. [2]

(b) Explain why the precipitate must be removed and why filtration alone, before adding washing soda, would not soften this water. [2]

(c) Explain the conclusions from equal water portions needing 8.0 cm³ soap before boiling, 3.0 cm³ after boiling, and 1.0 cm³ after boiling followed by washing-soda treatment and filtration. The soft-water control needs 1.0 cm³; soap concentration and endpoint are constant. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Carbonate ions from washing soda react with dissolved calcium ions to form insoluble calcium carbonate.

(b) Remove the suspended calcium carbonate by filtration to obtain clear treated water rather than leaving solid particles in it. Before precipitation, dissolved calcium ions pass through ordinary filter paper, so filtration alone does not soften the water.

(c) Boiling removes some hardness, so a temporary component was present. The boiled sample still needs more soap than the soft-water control, showing residual permanent hardness. The final treatment reduces soap demand to the control value, consistent with removal of that residual hardness under this test.
marking_guidance: Part a: Washing soda supplies carbonate ions (1).
Part a: Ca²⁺+CO3²⁻→CaCO3 removes dissolved calcium as a precipitate (1).
Part b: Remove the suspended calcium carbonate so the treated water is free of that solid precipitate (1).
Part b: Before precipitation, dissolved calcium ions pass through filter paper, so filtration alone leaves the hardness ions in solution (1).
Part c: 8.0 to 3.0 cm³ shows a component removable by boiling (1).
Part c: 3.0 exceeds the 1.0 cm³ control, so hardness remains after boiling (1).
Part c: Final 1.0 cm³ matches the control, supporting effective removal of the remaining hardness (1).

items.prompt:
(a) Plan a comparison of hardness for two water samples using soap solution. Include quantities, controlled procedure, a persistent-lather endpoint and how to interpret the data. [6]

(b) Draw labelled apparatus for measuring a 50.0 cm³ water portion and then adding soap solution in measured increments to a comparison tube. [2]

(c) State the initial and final burette readings for sample B from the learner scale panels in ![Learner stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-11-04-learner.svg). [2]

(d) Explain the conclusion about hardness from these results: equal 50.0 cm³ water portions require 2.0 cm³ soap for A and 6.0 cm³ for B, using the same soap and endpoint. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Measure equal 50.0 cm³ water portions into matching tubes. Add the same concentration of soap solution from a burette in measured increments, recording initial and final readings. Stopper and shake each for the same time and intensity after each addition, then observe whether lather remains for 30 s. Repeat trials and compare the soap volumes required. A larger volume indicates greater hardness because more soap reacts with dissolved calcium/magnesium before lasting lather forms. Keep water temperature, tube geometry and the lather criterion constant.

(b) A graduated 50 cm³ measuring cylinder supplies the water portion to a stoppered comparison tube. A burette containing soap solution is held vertically by a stand and clamp, with its tap and tip positioned for controlled addition into the tube. The stopper is removed during addition and fitted for shaking.

(c) Initial B reading 0.40 cm³; final B reading 6.40 cm³. The soap volume delivered is the difference, 6.00 cm³.

(d) B is harder because it needs more of the same soap solution for the same water volume and endpoint. Its calcium/magnesium ions remove more soap as insoluble scum before a lasting lather forms.
marking_guidance: Part a: Equal measured water volumes (1).
Part a: Same soap concentration (1).
Part a: Measured soap increments with volume record (1).
Part a: Standardised shaking (1).
Part a: Consistent persistent-lather endpoint, e.g. 30 s (1).
Part a: Compare soap volumes to infer hardness (1). Accept repetitions and sensible controls as supporting detail, not extra marks.
Part b: Labelled graduated vessel suitable for the water volume (1).
Part b: Labelled burette or other suitably graduated addition device arranged to add into comparison tube (1). Accept a calibrated syringe with a controlled dispensing method.
Part c: Initial 0.40 cm³, tolerance ±0.05 (1).
Part c: Final 6.40 cm³, tolerance ±0.05 (1). No separate mark for subtraction in this part.
Part d: B harder from larger matched-condition soap requirement (1).
Part d: Ca2+/Mg2+ react with/remove soap before lather (1).
